evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 中軸排版 × 條列優勢 × 親切人像，打造具信任感的家庭服務廣告 此類設計常見於家庭僱傭、照護服務、社區人力資源推廣，強調「貼心」、「可靠」與「細緻安排」，透過親切人像＋條列式文案＋明確 CTA，有效提升觀眾信任與行動率。 這張圖的設計優勢包括： ✔ 親切女性人像為視覺焦點，拉近觀眾距離，提升信賴感 ✔ 主標「為何選擇印傭？」使用問句形式吸引好奇，搭配綠色字體突顯主題 ✔ 條列式優勢（願意主動學廣東話、純樸、適應力強等）清楚展示服務特點 ✔ 輔助語句如「深受香港家庭喜愛」、「全面而貼心」強化品牌承諾與安心感 ✔ 咖啡棕＋白＋綠色配色方案，營造穩重、溫暖與自然的氛圍 🧠 設計原則： 1️⃣ 主標建議使用疑問句＋關鍵字配色 → 吸引觀看並突顯主題 2️⃣ 條列式資訊清晰展示服務內容，有利觀眾快速掌握重點 3️⃣ 人像選擇以自然微笑為佳，配色宜採用溫暖沉穩色調提升信任感 👉 Prompting 重點字詞：friendly helper agency poster, smiling Asian woman, warm natural tones, center aligned layout, checklist benefits, professional recruitment flyer design 📍Follow 我地，解鎖更多 AI 人才服務類設計靈感！ #AI設計教學 #家庭僱傭設計 #信任感視覺 #人像主視覺 #條列式文案排版 #服務行銷設計 #溫暖配色設計 #AI生成應用 #社會服務美學 #WhatsApp轉換率提升

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 插畫風 × 色塊構圖，打造親切活潑的健康保險印象 這類設計特別適合推廣健康保險、兒童醫療計劃或家庭守護產品，用「可愛化角色 × 圓潤色塊 × 重點強調詞」迅速傳達保障與信任。 這張圖的設計優勢包括： ✔ 主角人物以插畫風呈現，笑容親切，易於引起情感共鳴 ✔ 色塊搭配插畫元素，營造出守護感（盾牌、心形、星星） ✔ 重點詞如「真幫手」、「保障」、「抵到爆」以大字+對比色圈出 → 一眼抓住重點 ✔ 使用黃／紅／藍的鮮明對比色，視覺上活潑又不失專業 ✔ 文案語調具口語化親和力，例如「真幫手」、「抵到爆」，貼近大眾日常語言 🧠 設計原則： 1️⃣ 插畫角色需笑容自然，服裝與顏色呼應品牌形象 2️⃣ 色塊資訊排列應環繞主角形成守護意象 3️⃣ 強調「低月費」、「有保障」、「安心」等實用利益字眼 👉 Prompting 建議字詞：illustration girl insurance protector, pastel medical theme, health policy poster layout, cartoon graphic design with callout icons, bold text bubbles, kawaii style 📍Follow 我地，學習更多 AI x 設計教學！ #AI設計 #健康保險插畫風 #卡通風格排版 #色塊構圖 #社交媒體宣傳圖 #平面設計參考 #生成式美學 #InstaAgent作品 #品牌溝通視覺 #保險行銷設計

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 高端護膚 × 鉑金精華視覺 金屬質感 × 淨白背景，營造奢華與專業兼備的品牌形象 這張 3D 水光鉑金版宣傳圖，以 中央產品陳列 + 上方立體標題 + 下方功效列表 的布局，�將護膚品的高端與科技感透過金色、白色和柔光呈現，讓視覺重點集中於「黃金針」與奢華護膚概念。 🎨 設計亮點 - 色彩搭配：金色呼應產品定位，搭配米白與淡橙，營造溫潤奢華感 - 立體標題設計：「3D水光鉑金版」以拱形排列 + 投影效果，帶出層次感 - 產品擺放：由左至右呈現多種單品，呼應「系列套裝」概念 - 功效條列：以漸層橙底條列文字，讓受眾快速理解主要功效與產品組成 💡 行銷啟示 高端護膚產品的設計重點是「專業可信 + 質感呈現」。以整齊產品排布加上金屬質感配色，可以瞬間傳遞價值感，吸引對高效修護有需求的消費者。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我地，帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #護膚品設計 #高端美容 #水光針 #品牌視覺 #美容中心 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #美容產品 #行銷美學 #高端設計 #奢華護膚 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #精華液 #美容套裝 #護膚科技

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 復古中式插畫 × 花田夢幻背景 × 情感式文案 這類設計常見於懷舊食品品牌、地方手作小吃、節慶限定產品，藉由復古包裝與溫暖情境，喚起觀眾的童年記憶與情感投射。 這張圖的設計優勢包括： ✔ 主視覺採用老香港風格插畫湯包包裝，極具辨識度與懷舊感 ✔ 背景配以漫天花瓣飄落的花田場景，營造一種溫柔又夢幻的氣氛 ✔ 主標語「暖心暖胃 家的味道」句式對仗且直指情感核心 ✔ 副標「今晚記得返嚟飲湯」語氣親切自然，充滿本地情懷 ✔ 色調以紅橙黃為主，配合花海與湯色，強化溫暖安心的感覺 🧠 設計原則： 1️⃣ 善用復古中式圖騰 + 插畫元素 → 建立品牌文化與本地特色 2️⃣ 利用自然場景與情感語言 → 增強品牌的情緒共鳴力 3️⃣ 排版上主視覺居中，文字底置 → 突顯產品，穩定視覺 👉 Prompting 重點字詞：vintage Chinese soup packaging design, retro Hong Kong food label, dreamy flower field background, petals falling, warm nostalgic color tones, cinematic illustration ad layout 📍Follow 我地，發掘更多 AI 本地品牌風格設計靈感！ #AI設計教學 #懷舊包裝設計 #情感文案美學 #本地食品品牌 #AI創作靈感 #插畫風包裝 #湯包設計 #返屋企飲湯啦 #復古情懷 #生成式設計

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 高端醫美 × 極簡美肌視覺 暖金光暈 × 無瑕人像，營造專業與高端並存的品牌氛圍 這張皮秒激光宣傳圖，採用 左下機台 + 中央大面積人像 + 右上標題 的經典醫美構圖，�光滑膚質與柔焦背景呼應「淨透亮」療程效果，下方三個圓形賣點圖標（斑點 / 毛孔細紋 / 膚質不均）將痛點可視化，讓受眾一眼對號入座。 🎨 設計亮點 - 暖金 × 柔白主色調：金色象徵高端科技，白色傳遞潔淨專業 - 國際認證背書：美國FDA + 歐盟CE雙重認證，提升信任感 - 光束與漸層背景：塑造激光的速度感與精準感 - 圓形賣點設計：聚焦常見肌膚問題，強化一次改善的印象 💡 行銷啟示 醫美設計中，專業感與美感要並行。以高質感視覺承載信任背書，再放大低風險與多功效賣點，能有效提升轉化率。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我地，帶你拆解一張設計！ #AIx設計美學 #皮秒激光 #醫美設計 #美肌療程 #品牌視覺 #醫美廣告 #高端設計 #行銷美學 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #美容中心 #肌膚管理 #斑點改善 #毛孔細紋 #膚質改善 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 教育推廣 × 親子互動視覺 溫馨陪伴 × 粉彩色調，營造啟發與成長並存的品牌氛圍 這張幼兒教育課程宣傳圖，以 親子互動畫面 + 大標語 + 功效圖示分區 的結構呈現。 母親陪伴孩子閱讀的畫面傳遞「關懷與啟發」，搭配粉彩色塊和手繪元素，讓整體氛圍更溫暖親切。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主視覺人物：母女共讀畫面，直觀展現「親子互動」與「啟發潛力」 - 色彩基調：淡藍、米黃、粉色，帶出柔和親子氛圍 - 資訊設計：右側三個圓形標籤（認知、情緒、社交）條列學習收穫，清晰易懂 - 標題排版：「讓孩子從小啟發潛力！」粉紅描邊字體，吸睛又帶童趣 💡 行銷啟示 親子教育的視覺關鍵是「信任感 + 成長期待」。這張圖透過真實互動畫面與卡通化裝飾元素，建立專業又親切的品牌形象，讓家長更容易代入並相信課程價值。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，每週帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #教育行銷 #親子教育 #啟發潛能 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #幼兒課程 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #親子互動 #幼兒發展

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 健美塑形 × 都市極簡視覺 肌膚線條 × 柔光背景，塑造健康與專業並存的品牌印象 這張減肥塑形療程宣傳圖，採用 右側身體特寫 + 左側文字訊息 + 下方價錢強調 的行銷結構，�以緊緻線條與白色運動服凸顯健康身材目標，並以漸層色塊和金屬質感點綴，帶出高端感。 🎨 設計亮點 - 色彩搭配：白色運動服 × 柔灰背景傳遞純淨健康，搭配金屬金與粉橘價錢標籤增添吸睛度 - 視覺分區：上中下三層訊息結構——療程名稱、核心功效、價格優惠，方便快速吸收 - 文字層級：重點功效用深色粗體，形成明顯視覺對比，抓住注意力 - 價錢設計：金色圓框＋紅字價格，製造限時優惠的緊迫感 💡 行銷啟示 塑形療程的視覺重點不只是「瘦」，而是傳遞「緊緻健康」的生活方式。透過分層訊息結構與高端配色，可讓消費者在第一眼就被吸引，並迅速理解賣點與價格優惠。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，帶你拆解好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #塑形療程 #減肥療程 #健美身材 #品牌視覺 #美容中心 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #身體雕塑 #行銷美學 #高端設計 #瘦身塑形 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #優惠活動 #都市女性 #體態管理

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 家具品牌 × 極簡溫潤視覺 暖色木質 × 現代空間感，營造舒適與設計並存的家居氛圍 這張家具宣傳圖，以 實景客廳佈置 + 中英雙語標語 + 底部聯絡方式 的結構設計，傳達「家的故事由床開始」的品牌核心理念。 🎨 設計亮點 - 雙語標語：上方「Every Home Story Begins With A Bed.」與下方中文「家的故事 由一張床開始」呼應，突顯國際化品牌形象 - 色彩基調：淺木色 × 米白色，溫潤柔和，營造「高質感 × 放鬆感」的家居氛圍 - 空間佈局：沙發、餐桌、書架、燈光層次分明，營造現代簡約的生活品味 - 品牌背書：底部「30+年經驗｜本地品牌｜品質保證｜設計傳承」增強信任度 💡 行銷啟示 家具品牌設計的關鍵在於「氛圍營造 + 品牌故事」。這張圖不只是賣床，而是將床放進完整的家居生活場景，用故事化的方式引導消費者想像「家的感覺」。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，每週帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #家具品牌 #家居設計 #室內設計 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #家具廣告 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #極簡主義 #家居生活

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 物理治療 × 專業健康視覺 疼痛緩解 × 機能恢復，營造專業與信任兼備的品牌形象 這張五十肩物理治療宣傳圖，以 主題人物痛點表現 + 對比療效展示 + 專業資訊分區 的構圖，清楚傳達療程功效與品牌專業感。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主標題設計：「告別50肩，抬手不再卡住」以大字體強調痛點與成果對比，立即吸睛 - 視覺焦點：主角抓著肩膀皺眉的表情，明確傳達「疼痛感」；下方對比區塊展示「放鬆」與「舉手順暢」，視覺對比清晰 - 色彩基調：綠色 × 藍青色調象徵健康與修復，搭配局部黃色強調優惠與 CTA - 資訊分區：以「筋膜放鬆、消炎止痛」為兩大重點效果，配合人體結構圖與真實照片，兼具專業與真實感 - 信任標語：非入侵綜合理療、聚焦衝擊波、電磁波等關鍵技術詞彙，增強專業可信度 💡 行銷啟示 醫療健康類設計的核心在於「痛點直擊 + 專業信任」。這張圖透過動態表情、清晰療效對比和明確療程技術，讓受眾直觀感受到「這個療法真的有用」，有效促進諮詢與預約。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我地，帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #物理治療 #肩周炎 #五十肩 #健康設計 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #健康品牌 #治療推廣 #疼痛管理

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 中醫療程 × 溫潤自然視覺 產後護理 × 髮根重建，營造專業與關懷並存的品牌氛圍 這張中醫養髮宣傳圖，以 分區對比 + 插圖說明 + 暖色調設計 的方式呈現，讓觀者迅速理解「產後脫髮成因」與「治療方向」，整體兼具專業可信與溫柔照護感。 🎨 設計亮點 - 標題層級：「產後掉髮不是自然現象」以深棕描邊字強調警示感；副標「體虛型脫髮更難自癒」延伸問題深度 - 人物對比照：左側「脫髮焦慮」、右側「掉髮困擾」，情緒代入感強，建立共鳴 - 底部資訊分區：以三個圖示說明療程核心（補氣養血、調理脾腎、針灸疏通），結構簡潔、專業易懂 - 色彩基調：以米棕、杏膚與暖木紋為主，呼應「自然中醫 × 健康修復」的品牌調性 💡 行銷啟示 健康療程類設計的關鍵在於「專業可信 + 情緒共鳴」。這張圖以真實人物焦慮表情搭配中醫圖示概念，讓受眾立即產生信任感與需求感，是兼具教育與轉化力的高效組合。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我地，帶你拆解好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #中醫養髮 #產後脫髮 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #健康養生 #氣血調理 #脾腎調理 #針灸治療 #女性健康

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 未來創業 × 超現實主題視覺 夢想與科技交錯，營造啟發與思辨並存的氛圍 這張以「AI × 少年 × 創業未來」為主題的視覺作品，透過 象徵式構圖 + 超現實畫面 + 對比文字設計，傳達了科技時代下的新一代創造者精神。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主題構圖：中央高塔象徵「目標與引導」，兩側的宇宙通道象徵「無限可能」與「多維未來」，形成強烈的中心視覺焦點。 - 色彩層次：天空藍 × 金黃色田野 × 深藍宇宙形成三層對比，既現實又夢幻，呈現「理性與想像力並行」的氛圍。 - 人物視角：低視角的人物背影象徵探索與啟程，強化觀者的代入感與未來感。 💡 行銷啟示 科技品牌與創業內容的設計核心在於「啟發性 × 前瞻性」。這張作品以藝術化手法詮釋 AI 未來敘事，不是單純的科技展示，而是一場對「人與 AI 共創未來」的提問，非常適合用於思想品牌、創業論壇、或未來趨勢系列。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，每週帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #未來創業 #AIAgent #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #未來主義 #科技藝術 #創業靈感

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 教育留學 × 創意城市視覺 巴黎 × 布魯塞爾雙城構圖，營造國際化與時尚感兼具的品牌氛圍 這張設計以 地標構圖 + 模組化課程介紹 + 紫橙漸層配色 呈現，完美平衡了「專業教育」與「創意設計」的雙重調性。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主題構圖：上方巴黎鐵塔與布魯塞爾市政廳相互融合，象徵「雙城聯動」與「跨文化創作」。 - 色彩基調：紫色代表藝術與思辨、橙色象徵創造與熱情；兩者融合形成現代藝術教育的活力調性。 - 資訊分區：以三個圓形模組呈現課程重點（雙學位／國際認證／實踐導向），結構清晰且具節奏感。 - 視覺節奏：上半主題大標吸睛、下半人物照拉近親和度，學術感與人情味兼具。 - CTA設計：「立即報名」與底部聯絡資訊使用高飽和紫色強化行動導向，清晰又統一。 💡 行銷啟示 教育品牌的設計關鍵在於「專業感 × 夢想感」。這張圖透過歐洲城市意象結合課程模組化資訊呈現，不僅傳遞國際視野，也讓觀者即時感受到升學與職涯的可能性。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #教育設計 #藝術學院 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #國際教育 #創意設計學習 #留學推廣

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 工程服務 × 專業信任視覺 流程透明 × 品質保證，營造穩重可靠的品牌形象 這張「工程零爛尾」主題宣傳圖，以 標題強對比 + 流程分區 + 實景團隊照 的結構設計，傳達企業長期穩健與專業可信的品牌印象。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主標題設計：以大字體「為何我們16年的工程零爛尾？」開場，強烈引發信任與好奇，形成品牌背書感 - 配色基調：深藍 × 銀灰 × 金橙的專業配色，象徵穩重、信任與高品質 - 視覺焦點：中段團隊討論照片展現企業文化與專業氛圍，真實自然 - 流程設計：下方以三階段流程（設計 → 報價及施工 → 工程）呈現服務透明度 - 認證背書：右下 ISO9001 認證圖示，視覺化呈現專業品質標準 💡 行銷啟示 B2B 工程設計的關鍵在於「信任 + 專業體系」。這張圖透過「16年經驗」與「標準化流程」雙重背書，加上 ISO 認證與真實團隊畫面，有效建立企業可信度與品牌權威。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #工程設計 #品牌視覺 #企業行銷 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #企業品牌 #B2B行銷 #專業信任

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 汽車科技 × 高對比專業視覺 360°全景 × 智能監控，營造安全感與科技感並存的品牌氛圍 這張汽車環景系統宣傳圖，以 實際畫面展示 + 高對比配色 + 功能分區圖示 的構圖呈現，突出產品的「零死角安全體驗」。 🎨 設計亮點 - 標題設計：主標「零死角AR360」採用亮黃配深藍描邊，強烈對比形成科技聚焦感；上方問題式開場「停車視野有限？馬上升級」增加行動誘因 - 視覺焦點：中央以真實駕駛畫面展示車機螢幕，突顯「實景功能」的可信度與科技感 - 色彩基調：藍 × 黃為主色，傳遞「科技 × 安全」印象，與汽車品牌常用色調一致 - 資訊分區：底部以四大功能模組（全景影像、四鏡頭錄影、四小時錄影、夜視功能）對稱排列，資訊清晰、層次分明 - 品牌信任感：下方展示多款車廠品牌Logo（Mercedes、BMW、Audi、Honda等），加強兼容性與專業印象 💡 行銷啟示 汽車科技行銷的核心是「安全 + 專業可信」。這張設計以真實畫面增強信任，以明亮色塊與清晰功能分區提升可讀性，有效平衡技術細節與視覺吸引力，是科技產品推廣中極具參考價值的排版方式。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #汽車科技 #全景影像 #行車安全 #品牌視覺 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #科技設計 #行銷美學 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #汽車升級 #智能駕駛

evidence.authorName: 📌 AI x 設計美學 汽車品牌 × 情境式防災視覺 暴雨風球 × 出車貼士，營造專業與信任兼具的品牌形象 這張宣傳圖以 真實天氣場景 + 情境式文案 + 溫馨提醒布局 呈現，成功把「品牌專業」與「顧客關懷」結合成具信任感的行銷素材。 🎨 設計亮點 - 主題設計：「遇上暴雨風球 點算好？」以大字白字配深色雨景背景，強烈對比下瞬間抓住眼球 - 場景氛圍：真實雨天車輛實拍，雨滴與濕地反光讓畫面具臨場感，傳遞「實戰應用」氛圍 - 配色基調：深灰 × 墨綠 × 黃色強調標籤，呈現穩重又醒目的品牌語調 - 資訊結構：分為兩大模組——「出車安排」與「溫馨貼士」，用直線分隔條保持視覺秩序 💡 行銷啟示 汽車品牌內容行銷的關鍵在於「功能之外的信任連結」。這張圖透過天氣應變情境教育，巧妙轉化為品牌責任與專業象徵，在建立信任的同時，也潛移默化強化品牌記憶度。 📲 想看更多品牌設計靈感？Follow 我們，每週帶你拆解一張好設計！ #AIx設計美學 #汽車品牌 #暴雨風球 #品牌視覺 #行銷美學 #品牌設計靈感 #視覺行銷 #設計靈感 #廣告設計解析 #商業設計 #品牌塑造 #設計美感 #汽車安全 #情境行銷 #AutoBright

People aren’t reacting to “better visuals” — they’re reacting to believability. This feels like the moment AI video finally crossed the line. evidence.originalText:
AI isn’t replacing programming, but it has changed what a 10x engineer looks like. How many tokens does your best engineer use every month? How many of your engineers are still writing code manually without AI?

Our bet is that the same trend will take place for knowledge work.

There is a huge upside for any knowledge worker in learning how to interact with AI: From thinking critically about what they want the AI to do, prompting it properly, to parallelizing and queuing work.

In many organizations, that is already happening. The big transition will come when teams start sharing and improving their skills across the organization.

You'll be able to get a pulse of what happened while you were OOO with an automation, build a deck with the taste of your best UI designer or fill a form quicker than Shannon from accounting.

evidence.title: Six months ago, a mid-market lender got a routine LP data request.
evidence.text:
Six months ago, a mid-market lender got a routine LP data request.

"Can you pull the confirmation records for the supply chain facilities from Q4?"

Standard ask. Thirty-minute job, they assumed.

Four business days later, they were still reconstructing.

The confirmation records existed... 
somewhere, but, where?)

Spread across three email inboxes, two shared drives, a folder labeled "2025 Verification Misc," and a spreadsheet someone had built to track things manually before realizing it was too slow to maintain. The analyst who had run most of those confirmations was on parental leave.

They found what they needed. Eventually. But the LP had moved on and was now asking a different question: not about Q4, but about their verification process in general.

ABF Journal covered a version of this story in a different context last week, noting that "documentation, audit rights and confirmation protocols are all being rebuilt" across the asset class following verification gaps that surfaced in supply chain financing last year. The exposure wasn't the fraud itself. It was the absence of a clean, timestamped record of what the lender had checked and when.

What LP due diligence looks like now is different from what it looked like two years ago. The question has shifted from "do you have the data?" to "can you show me the process that produced it?"

A spreadsheet answer to that question used to be acceptable.

It isn't anymore.

The operations that can answer that question in minutes rather than days aren't running harder. They're running with a different system: one where the verification record is created automatically at the moment of confirmation, not reconstructed four days later when someone asks.

Leave audit trails to Zolvo, hit us up at hi@zolvo.com

evidence.title: "Private Credit in 2026: Discipline, Dispersion and Defaults" by Arcesium makes a point operators already suspect: default outcomes get decided long before the default shows up on
evidence.text:
"Private Credit in 2026: Discipline, Dispersion and Defaults" by Arcesium  makes a point operators already suspect: default outcomes get decided long before the default shows up on paper, in how early the operational team notices stress and how fast that signal reaches the right person.

Most servicing teams already have that signal. It just doesn't travel.

A collections analyst notices a borrower asking for three payment extensions in six weeks. Notes it in the CRM. Moves to the next call.

A reconciliation analyst, working a different queue entirely, notices the same borrower's payments have started arriving four to six days late, every month, for the last quarter.

Neither analyst sees the other's notes. Neither one is wrong. The information just lives in two systems that don't talk, updated by two people who don't compare notes unless something has already gone wrong enough to force a meeting.

By the time both signals reach a risk officer together, the borrower isn't early-stage stressed anymore. They're 60 days out, and the workout conversation starts from a weaker position than it needed to.

The whitepaper's framing: technology integration matters less as a productivity story and more as a signal-routing story. The extension requests and the late payments were never separate data points. They were the same borrower, in the same quarter, telling the same story twice, to two people who never compared notes.

Fixing this isn't hiring a risk analyst to read every note. It's making the collections log and the reconciliation ledger reference the same borrower record, so the pattern surfaces on its own instead of waiting for a human to notice it twice.

How are you preventing or solving this gap?🧐

evidence.title: What should we talk about when focusing on niche lending: construction, oilfield services, staffing?
evidence.text:
What should we talk about when focusing on niche lending: construction, oilfield services, staffing?

SFNet's panel spent an hour on one idea: the red flags in these industries don't look like red flags anywhere else.

A regional factor decided to test that against their own book. They ran an audit on 90 days of construction invoices.

What they found:

One: pay-if-paid clauses buried in subcontracts that made half their "eligible" receivables conditional on a payment that hadn't happened yet.

Two: three invoices from the same GC, same project, submitted by two different subcontractors they were funding. Same job, same money, funded twice.

Three: a staffing sub-vertical where the invoice amount tracked headcount that didn't match any payroll filing on record.

None of these tripped a standard fraud check. Standard checks look for forged documents and inflated amounts. These were real documents, real numbers, wrong assumptions.

The panel's point: construction, oilfield, and staffing all carry industry-specific structures, retainage, joint checks, pay-if-paid, per diem staffing math, that a generic verification process was never built to catch.

The factor's fix wasn't more review time. It was industry-specific rules layered onto the standard checks: flag pay-if-paid language automatically, cross-reference GC and project across submissions, tie staffing invoices to headcount data.

Same team. Same volume. Different questions being asked of every invoice.

evidence.title: ABF Journal's read on this week: higher-for-longer cost of capital, collateral-anchored underwriting, borrowing-base discipline.
evidence.text:
ABF Journal's read on this week: higher-for-longer cost of capital, collateral-anchored underwriting, borrowing-base discipline. That's the environment every commercial lender is underwriting into right now.

Here's the number that environment doesn't show up in, but should: what your current manual servicing process is costing you per month, separate from your cost of capital.

Take a mid-size factoring shop running $80M in receivables. Three reconciliation analysts at $75K a year. If 40% of their time goes to fixing errors and rework instead of new volume, that's roughly $90,000 a year spent correcting a process instead of running it.

Add invoice fraud that slips past manual review because a 60-invoice batch doesn't get six layers of checking, it gets two. Add a borrowing base certificate that's a week behind the actual reconciled ledger by the time an LP or auditor asks for it.

None of that shows up as a line item. It shows up as a slower close, a covenant question nobody can answer cleanly, and a fraud loss that gets discovered eighteen months later in a portfolio review.

In a higher-for-longer environment, capital is already more expensive. Layering an unmeasured servicing cost on top of that is a choice, even when it doesn't feel like one.

The question worth asking this quarter: if reconciliation, invoice verification, and borrowing-base reporting ran on current data instead of last week's export, what would that actually be worth against the cost of capital already being paid?

Asset-based lending and factoring businesses run on heavily siloed core platforms, manual spreadsheet validation, fragmented email workflows, and disconnected communication channels. When you try to add AI on top of that foundation, you're trying to automate a broken process instead of fixing the process itself.

The result: AI becomes a nice-to-have feature instead of the operating model.

The teams that moved first weren't the ones with the most capital or the biggest development budgets. They were the ones willing to look at their infrastructure honestly and say: this is the problem, and we need to solve it before automation makes sense.

What does that fix look like?

- Unified payment data flow from bank to reconciliation to LP reporting, not three separate spreadsheets
- Invoice verification and fraud detection running on every submission, not on the ones an analyst decides to check
- Collections outreach prioritized by risk and amount, not by whoever remembered to follow up
- An audit trail that exists by default, not something you reconstruct after an incident

The cost of not fixing infrastructure:
- Headcount that scales proportionally with portfolio growth (you hit a wall)
- Month-end closes that take 8-12 days instead of 2-3
- Fraud and errors that stay hidden until LP audit
- AI pilots that never move to production because they're trying to solve a people problem with a technology fix

If you're managing $20M+ in AUM and you're still reconciling manually or on spreadsheets: this is costing you more than you think.

evidence.originalText:
82% of commercial lenders reported rising fraud losses.

More than one-third experienced double-digit increases year-over-year. But here's what matters: almost all of that fraud passed initial document review.

Most lenders are running one verification layer on invoice submissions. Format check, amount plausibility, a visual scan for obvious inconsistencies. That catches the amateur stuff: the sloppy forgeries, the typos, the invoices that scream "fake."

What it misses: circular fraud, where two entities controlled by the same actor create invoices between themselves. Multi-lender pledging, where the same invoice gets submitted to three lenders on the same day. Backdated documents, where metadata contradicts the stated history but the visual is clean.

These aren't rare edge cases. They're engineered specifically to survive a human review in under 5 minutes.

The economic consequence is direct: a funded fraudulent invoice is a realized loss, not a write-down risk. No spread covers it. And when the LP audit asks for the evidence trail, if you were running a visual review only, the trail stops at "looked OK."

The lenders catching sophisticated fraud are running 4 to 6 layers: document surface validation, buyer registry verification, relationship plausibility checks, cross-portfolio duplicate detection, metadata analysis, and accounts payable corroboration.

Most operations teams can't run all six layers manually at volume. So the first move is systematic: stop treating verification as a judgment call. Define which checks run on every invoice. Then automate the ones taking more than 10 minutes per document.

evidence.originalText:
Your reconciliation team is spending 40% of their time fixing errors from prior months.

That's the number that keeps appearing in operational audits: teams that reconcile manually dedicate 40-60% of their capacity to rework: payment misapplications, incorrectly decomposed wires, borrower-to-loan mismatches discovered after posting.

Here's why this matters: Numeric's research from May this year showed that manual reconciliation extends a month-end close by up to four additional days. A financial consolidation study found that the cost of manual reconciliation errors for mid-market firms often exceeds $60,000 per reporting cycle.

That's not a typo. It's sixty thousand usd. In one month.

The root cause is process fragmentation. Bank data lives in one system, invoices in another, remittance details scattered across email and spreadsheets. A payment arrives untagged or with incomplete reference data. An analyst spends 20 minutes figuring out which borrower it belongs to. One mismatch hides in a cell. The cascade starts: loan-level balances don't reconcile to the GL, collateral calculations are off by $50K, the LP data tape goes out with an exception flag attached.

The operational consequence: a team spending a quarter of its time on preventable work instead of exception management.

The path forward isn't adding headcount. It's moving from "review everything" to "match systematically, review exceptions." When payment matching runs at 87% confidence or higher automatically, your team shifts from reconciliation to validation.

The benchmark difference is visible: teams using systematic matching and exception-based review close in 2-3 days. Teams running fully manual processes typically close in 8-12 days.

evidence.title:
The big defense primes are optimized for a world that's in peace.

High-margin. Low-volume. Cost-plus contracts. That model printed money...
evidence.text:
The big defense primes are optimized for a world that's in peace.

High-margin. Low-volume. Cost-plus contracts. That model printed money for 20 years, but the defense industry is shifting from contract-based to product-based procurement, and that changes everything.

Why pay $5M per missile when you can get like-minded specs for under $100K?

You can't cost-engineer your way out of a structural problem. These companies aren't slow because of bad management, they're slow because their entire machine was built to be slow. That's how you maximize margin on a 10-unit order.

The future belongs to whoever can produce at scale, at speed, and at price. That's not a prime. That's a product company. 

@anduriltech is like the ferrari of the defense industry, high-precision instruments.

My company Tenet Industries is building the Toyota; high-volume, mass-produced at scale. Rapidly deployable.

Microgravity, unlimited vacuum, and 24/7 solar energy create conditi...
evidence.text:
The next frontier of manufacturing is not on Earth. It is in orbit.

Microgravity, unlimited vacuum, and 24/7 solar energy create conditions that are physically impossible to replicate at scale on the ground. Industries like semifabs stand to benefit enormously from these properties. Space manufacturing could break through the physical constraints that laws like Moore's Law are running into right now. New physics environments unlock new performance ceilings.

But here is the hard problem nobody is talking about (highlighted by Andurils post).

Defending assets on Earth benefits from geography and detection time. A missile launched from a hostile nation gives you time to respond. A satellite passing over adversarial territory has none of that buffer. The threat geometry is entirely different. Intercept windows are narrow. Response latency needs to be near-zero (or even fucking negative).

Latency becomes the big problem.

We need to rethink defensive architecture from the ground up for orbital assets. Not adapt existing frameworks. Actually rebuild them for the environment. 

The economic case for space manufacturing is becoming real. The strategic and security infrastructure to protect it has to develop in parallel, not as an afterthought.

This is something we're working on as our next domain for Tenet.

evidence.text: Is it possible to ship an AI agent that follows the team's best-practice playbook, but still adapts to how each CSM actually works? They encode what's actually working across your customer base, and you don't want every CSM improvising their own version. But rigid tools get annoying to customize every time. Each person layers their own preferences on top. Best practice stays intact. Personal workflow gets respected. Nobody has to pick a side.

The last outbound tool you’ll ever need. We’re GojiberryAI. And outbound will never work the same way again.

evidence.title: Tracking customers' MCP usage
evidence.text: Everybody's launching MCP. Nobody's measuring its adoption. Which is wild, because MCP isn't a small bet. If it's wrong, you've shipped a feature into a black box. Userlens (YC P26) treats MCP like any other surface. We capture which customers have connected it, which users inside those customers are actually invoking tools, and which specific tool calls are being made. Read vs. write. Exploration vs. real workflow. How it shifts week over week. Same fidelity you'd expect from product analytics on your core app, just applied to the AI surface most teams have left uninstrumented. Userlens flagged the stall, recommended next steps, and drafted outreach to turn those two power users into champions for the rest of the team. This is what "AI-native CS" actually looks like in practice. Not a chatbot on a dashboard. Real visibility into the surfaces your customers are betting on, with the agent doing the work of figuring out what to do about it.

evidence.authorName: How to benchmark users' adoption and what to do with the data
evidence.title: How to benchmark users' adoption and what to do with the data
evidence.text: If you have customers using MCP, there's one question worth more than any roadmap meeting: which of them is using it best, and why? Most CS teams can't actually answer that. They have anecdotes from their top CSM. They have feature usage data scattered across dashboards. What they don't have is a clean read on which accounts are leading, which are stalling, and what the leaders are doing differently. With Userlens (YC P26), you can. That's what benchmarking unlocks. But the real value isn't the leaderboard. It's the next question. What are the leading accounts doing that the stalled ones aren't? And can I package that into a playbook for the rest of the book? That's where Userlens goes from "reporting tool" to "adoption engine." Concrete plays for expanding the accounts that are winning, and concrete plays for bringing back the ones drifting. The ultimate goal isn't a dashboard. It's driving adoption, driving consumption, helping customers unlock value, and growing revenue as the byproduct of doing that well.

evidence.title: We Raised $4.8M to Build ChatGPT for Explainer Videos
evidence.text: We raised $4.8M to build Lamina Labs and make AI explain with video, not just text. Our first product is Simi, named after my lovely village, Simikot. Simi is ChatGPT for explainer videos. Give it a single prompt, document, article, PDF, slide deck, script, or workflow, and it generates a complete narrated whiteboard-style explainer video. On the fastest tier, a one-minute video can be ready in under 20 seconds. Simi works in 80+ languages and handles the script, visuals, animation, and narration. Simi can be used for: • Course lessons and educational videos • Employee onboarding and internal training • Customer training and education • Product walkthroughs and startup explainers • Technical and research breakdowns • Turning articles, documents, and presentations into videos • Generating explainer videos directly inside another product through our API Kartikesh and I were born in two of the most remote parts of Nepal. Neither of us grew up knowing what MIT, Y Combinator, or venture capital were. Somehow, we both made it to MIT, met there, and became the first all-Nepalese founding team in Y Combinator history. Today, we are announcing a $4.8 million seed round for Lamina Labs, led by Foundation Capital, with participation from Link Ventures and Y Combinator. We are building video infrastructure for LLMs so that any model, agent, or application can explain with video, not just text. Try Simi for free: https://laminalabs.ai #AI #ExplainerVideos #Startup

evidence.text: Handing out subscriptions to everyone doesn't mean your business will get value from AI. The hard part is getting your team to use it well. Rakesh, CEO of Piping Technology & Products, shows it doesn't have to be that hard. On a Sunday, Piping Technology CEO Rakesh Agrawal tried Tasklet for the first time. By Monday afternoon, he had called an emergency onboarding for nine employees. Forty days later, more than 60 team members were using agents to triage email, review contracts, prepare reports, follow up on orders, and accelerate quoting—all by describing the work in plain English. evidence.text:
Your broker and a fiduciary are held to different standards. Most employers assume they're the same thing.

A broker has to offer suitable options. A fiduciary has a legal duty to act in your interest, which means disclosing how they're paid and why they recommended what they did.

Most benefits brokers are not fiduciaries. That's not misconduct, it's how the arrangement is built. But it changes what you can reasonably expect.

A PEO bundles benefits into its broader service. An HRIS lets you manage your HR functions without tying your health plan to the system.

That difference can affect which plans you offer, how you shop for coverage, and how much visibility you have into what you're paying.

So don't choose based on HR features alone. Look at what each option means for your benefits, too.

evidence.title:
Why are legal services broken?

Not because lawyers lack value, but because the traditional legal services model often neglects the client experience.

For many clients, the process is difficult to navigate from the start. Pricing is unclear, timelines uncertain, and communication slow. Clients are often asked to make important decisions without fully understanding the process, the cost, or the expected outcome.

What makes this harder is that many of these issues are treated as normal features of the legal industry.

Hourly billing. Long back and forth processes. Limited visibility. Heavy reliance on referrals. Complex language and unclear next steps.

For clients, these are not features of the system. They are bugs in the experience. 

They create uncertainty, increase costs, and make legal support feel inaccessible to the people and businesses that need it most.

At Index Law, we believe legal services should be redesigned with the client experience as the priority.

This means clearer pricing, faster guidance, transparent processes, and access to qualified legal professionals when human expertise is needed.

The emergence of AI gives us the infrastructure to rethink how legal solutions are delivered. It can reduce repetitive work, organize complex information, identify key issues faster, and help clients understand what happens next.

The opportunity is not just to make law firms more efficient.
It is to make legal services clearer, more accessible, and more client-first.

https://indexlaw.com/

evidence.title:
The Cost Of Legal Uncertainty

Legal uncertainty is expensive.

Not just because of legal fees, but because of what happens while waiting for clarity.

A deal gets delayed. A launch is pushed back. A founder avoids making a decision. An investor asks a question the company cannot answer confidently.

Often, the legal issue itself is manageable. The real problem is not knowing how serious it is, what the options are, or how long it will take to resolve.
That uncertainty creates friction across the business.

Good legal support should eliminate that friction. It should help clients understand where they stand, what needs to happen next, and how they can move forward with confidence.

That is where AI will make a real difference.

At Index Law, we use our AI-native systems to organize information, identify key issues, and reduce the time spent on repetitive legal work. This allows our network of legal professionals to focus on judgment, strategy, and execution.

The value is not simply faster legal work.

It is giving clients the clarity they need to make decisions, protect momentum, and keep moving forward.

evidence.title: Info-Tech's new CMO Playbook lists six challenges defining the modern CMO job. Two of them sit right next to each other: increased revenue accountability and fragmented attribution.
evidence.text:
Info-Tech's new CMO Playbook lists six challenges defining the modern CMO job. Two of them sit right next to each other: increased revenue accountability and fragmented attribution.

Put those together and you get the actual problem. Marketing is being held to a revenue number using a measurement system that can't cleanly show which activity produced it. That's not a marketing failure. That's being graded on an exam nobody can score.

If you're building an internal case for anything right now, budget, headcount, a new program, don't lead with the activity. Lead with the piece you can actually trace to a deal. One traceable line beats five impressive ones finance can't verify.

evidence.title:
Waste Management took 984 collection routes off the road in nine months, and saved $18 million that year.

After a run of acquisitions, WM had the largest waste fleet in North America, about 26,000 vehicles serving ten million homes, with routing done district by district. One manager described his tools as highlighters, string, pushpins and maps cut up and pasted together.

In March 2003 WM began rolling out WasteRoute, a route-management system built with the Institute of Information Technology. It re-sequences every stop in a district and tells dispatchers how many trucks the work really needs. A re-route that used to take six to twelve months took four weeks.

What changed:
- 984 fewer routes by the end of 2003
- $18 million saved in 2003, by WM's estimate
- $44 million projected for 2004

Each route is a truck, a driver, fuel and maintenance. WM put it at about $10,000 a month.

It was a finalist for the 2004 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of routing model for a fleet of 20 trucks or 200, built in weeks on the data a dispatcher already has.

If your routes are still drawn with a highlighter, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
Air New Zealand replaced two weeks of manual rostering with an hour of computing, and saved about NZ$15.7 million a year doing it.

An airline has to decide which sequence of flights each crew member flies, with rest rules, bases, aircraft types and the crew's own preferences all in play. In 1984 Air New Zealand made every one of those decisions by hand. Building a roster took six people two weeks.

Over 13 years, from 1986 to 1999, the airline's planners and the University of Auckland built eight optimization systems covering every part of the problem: which tours of duty to fly, and who flies them, for pilots and flight attendants, domestic and international.

What changed, by the authors' count:
- NZ$15,655,000 a year saved
- rosters for all crew ranks and all bases built in under four person-days; the optimization runs themselves take less than an hour
- rosters that better respect what the crew asked for, not just the cost

It was a finalist for the 2000 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a plant's shifts or a fleet's drivers, built in weeks on the data the operation already has.

If your roster still takes a planner a fortnight, we'd like to hear how it gets built.

It did not start that way. First, experienced dispatchers assigned orders by hand. Then software assigned them one at a time, and service got worse as volume grew. Then it batched them area by area, which was fast enough but no longer good enough.

In 2019 Meituan's own team, working with researchers at Tsinghua University, put in a system that plans a whole city at once. Machine learning estimates how each courier will move, and an optimization model commits to the assignments.

What changed, comparing 2022 with 2019:
- delivery time per order down 20.96 percent
- courier travel distance per order down 23.77 percent
- orders delivered per full-time courier per day up more than 109 percent
- about $230 million a year in lower costs, by the authors' estimate

It was a finalist for the 2023 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a dispatch desk with 40 drivers, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team still assigns jobs one at a time as they come in, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.title:
Molslinjen runs 21 ferries on 10 routes in Denmark and carries about 15 million guests a year. Every departure has a fixed car deck, and the tickets for it go on sale long before anyone knows who will show up.

In 2020 it put a forecasting and revenue management system into operation, built with the Danish analytics firm Halfspace. It predicts the passengers and vehicles of each type for every departure up to a year ahead, and keeps updating until the ferry sails. From that forecast it decides how many tickets to offer in each category, what the reduced fares should cost within a set range, and how to pack vehicles on the car deck.

What changed, by the estimates in the award entry:
- 15 to 20 million Danish kroner in extra profit a year, about $2.6 to $3.2 million
- 3 percent less fuel and emissions
- more usable capacity on each departure and fewer delayed departures

It won the 2024 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: a forecast that keeps updating and a model that commits to a plan around it, built in weeks on the data an operation already has.

If your team sets prices or capacity close to the date because nothing looks that far ahead, we'd like to hear how you handle it.

evidence.title:
General Motors gained more than $2.1 billion in added revenue and savings by working out, plant by plant, which point on the line was holding back the rest.

A car plant is a long chain of stations with small stocks of unfinished cars between them. When one station stops, the ones after it run dry and the ones before it fill up. The plant makes only as many cars as its slowest point allows.

In the late 1980s GM started a long-term project of its own to predict the throughput of its production lines and improve it. It had three parts. Models that estimate how much a line will produce, find the bottleneck and decide how much buffer to hold between stations. Plant-floor systems that collect data in real time to feed those models. And one common process for turning what the models find into improvements, both when a line is designed and while it runs.

What changed, by GM's count, as published in 2006:
- more than $2.1 billion in added revenue and savings
- in more than 30 vehicle plants
- across 10 countries

It won the 2005 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a plant with one line and a few dozen stations, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team knows the line is losing output but not which station to fix first, we'd like to hear how you decide.

evidence.title:
Swift & Company, then the third-largest beef and pork processor in the United States, paid back its scheduling model twice over in the first year.

A beef plant has one input it cannot change, the carcass, and hundreds of outputs it can. Which cuts to make from each one, at which of five plants, in which shift, depends on the orders in hand, the prices of the day and what the plant can physically do. Promising a customer a delivery date on top of that was guesswork, or in the company's own words, anecdotal knowledge.

With Aspen Technology, Swift built a system of 45 linear programs on three model formulations. It reschedules the five plants in real time as orders arrive, and it tells sales what date it can promise on a new order, then holds the plan to that promise.

What changed, by Swift's own account:
- a 200 percent return on investment in the first year of production
- better order fulfilment and on-time delivery, and more of each week's production already sold before it was made
- the INFORMS release at the time put it at 13 percent added to bottom-line profit

It was a finalist for the 2005 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a food plant with one site, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your plant's weekly cut plan still depends on who is in the room on Monday, we'd like to hear how it gets made.

evidence.title:
Netherlands Railways rebuilt its entire timetable from scratch and added an estimated €40 million a year in profit on the same tracks.

The old timetable dated from 1970. Passenger traffic had nearly doubled since, and freight was up 285 percent. NS kept adding trains to the old structure until the buffers were gone and the delays piled up. Building more track instead would have cost about €10 billion through 2020.

So NS did something railways almost never do: it started again. Its own planners, working with university researchers, generated timetables for about 5,500 daily trains with optimization models and let the board choose between them. The same tools then scheduled the rolling stock and the roughly 6,000 crew members, work that had always been done by hand.

What changed, by NS's own estimates:
- about €40 million a year in extra profit: €30 million from more efficient train and crew schedules, €10 million from more passengers
- punctuality up from 84.8 percent in 2006 to 87.0 percent in 2007, a record at the time
- crew scheduling that used to start a year ahead now starts three months ahead

It won the 2008 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a fleet, a plant or a crew roster, built in weeks on the data the operation already has.

If your schedule still rests on a structure nobody has rebuilt in years, we'd like to hear how you plan around it.

evidence.title:
Sears ran its delivery and home-service fleets on a routing model it credited with over $42 million a year in savings.

Every evening Sears built the next day's routes for more than 1,000 delivery trucks and 12,500 service vans: which stops, in which order, inside the time window each customer had been promised. Technicians repair and install appliances and do home improvements; a wrong sequence means a missed window.

In the 1990s Sears and the mapping company ESRI built a system that puts a map engine under a vehicle-routing model. It computes the travel times between every pair of stops, assigns the work to vehicles and technicians by skill and schedule, then sequences and improves each route.

What changed, by Sears's count:
- over $42 million a year in savings
- over $9 million in one-time savings
- on-time performance up, miles between stops down, more customers per truck per day, less overtime

It was a finalist for the 1998 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of dispatch model for a service company with 20 vans or 200, built in weeks on the data the dispatcher already has.

If your technicians' day is still built by hand the evening before, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
Hewlett-Packard added more than $500 million in profit by deciding, with a model, which products to launch and which to focus on.

Variety sells, and it costs. Every near-identical product adds demand volatility, worse forecasts, more inventory, longer order cycles and more confused customers. HP found its product lines were sometimes driving business to competitors.

The company built two tools. The first screens every proposed new product with a return-on-investment calculator before launch; below the threshold, it does not ship. The second, Revenue Coverage Optimization, uses a maximum-flow algorithm to find the core set of products that covers most of the order book, so operations can concentrate on those.

What changed, by HP's count:
- more than $500 million in profit improvement across its businesses since 2005
- a leaner offering, faster delivery and lower overhead
- higher customer satisfaction and market share

It won the 2009 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a manufacturer with 300 SKUs instead of 30,000, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your catalogue has grown by addition and never by subtraction, we'd like to hear how you decide what stays.

evidence.title:
Chile feeds 1.3 million schoolchildren from low-income families every day. Since 1997 it has decided who cooks the meals with an optimization model.

The state spends about US$180 million a year on the contracts, one of the largest public auctions in the country. Until 1997 the contracts were awarded by a committee grading technical proposals and filtering bids by hand. Price played little part, and the authors of the study are blunt about the result: a lot of money for low-quality food, and officials under pressure from bidders.

JUNAEB, the agency in charge, worked with the University of Chile to redesign the auction. Caterers now bid on packages of territories, so a firm can offer a better price for regions it can serve together. An integer program with over 10,000 binary variables picks the combination of bids that meets quality standards at the lowest total cost. In the 2000 round it chose among 12,000 bids and found the optimum, which the authors note was anything but easy.

What changed, by the authors' estimate:
- meal quality rose, and the price per meal came in roughly 22 percent below what the trend predicted for that quality
- the authors put that at around US$40 million a year, the cost of feeding 300,000 children
- a transparent process that firms could not lobby their way through

The case is cited in Paul Milgrom's book on auction design, the work that won him the 2020 Nobel Prize in economics.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a buyer or a plant with far fewer bids and no university on call, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your biggest contracts are still awarded by committee, we'd like to hear how the decision gets made.

evidence.title:
Alibaba saves about $55 million a year with routing models that have only seconds to answer.

Its grocery chain Freshippo guarantees delivery in 30 minutes or less to customers within three kilometers of a store. Most route planning assumes every order is known in advance and the model has an hour or two to run. Here orders keep arriving, and each decision has to be made seconds after an order is placed, so that the picking and the driving get the rest of the half hour.

Alibaba's own operations research team built a set of routing algorithms for this. In a Freshippo store they decide which orders are picked together, the route each picker takes through the back-end warehouse, and which driver delivers which batch in what sequence. One method searches for better routes inside a four-second limit. Another is a neural network trained offline that returns a route almost instantly.

What changed, by the authors' count, published in 2022:
- about $55 million a year in savings across five Alibaba businesses, added up from field experiments
- transport costs down 4.3 percent on average
- at Freshippo the model is called almost half a million times a day

It was a finalist for the 2021 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of routing model for a warehouse with ten pickers or a fleet of 30 vans, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team plans the routes once in the morning and adjusts by phone for the rest of the day, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.title:
In 2021 Lyft changed how it matches drivers to riders, and the share of ride requests it could not find a driver for fell 13 percent.

Lyft already matched in batches. Every few seconds it gathered the open requests and the available drivers and solved for the best set of pairs. But each match was judged on that moment alone. Where the trip would leave the driver afterwards, and what that driver could earn there, did not count.

Lyft's own team, working with Sébastien Martin of Northwestern University, added that missing piece. The system estimates in real time what a driver can expect to earn from any place at any hour, keeps learning as conditions change, and feeds that value into every matching decision. Lyft tested it in 2021 by switching it on and off hour by hour in its markets, then rolled it out everywhere it operates.

What changed, as measured in Lyft's experiments:
- ride requests with no driver found down 13 percent
- rider cancellations down 3 percent
- five-star ratings up 1 percent
- more than $30 million a year in incremental revenue, by Lyft's internal estimate

It was a finalist for the 2023 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a dispatch desk with 40 vehicles, one that counts where each vehicle will be after the job, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team sends the nearest free vehicle to each job, we'd like to hear how you do it.

evidence.title:
American Airlines estimated it earned $1.4 billion of extra revenue in three years without adding a single seat. It changed how it decided which seats to sell at which price.

A seat on a flight is worth nothing once the door closes. Sell too many cheap seats early and the late business traveller finds the flight full. Hold too many back and they fly empty. American began working on the problem in the early 1960s and launched discount fares in 1977, which made it urgent.

Its decision-technologies group broke the problem into three models it could actually solve: how many seats to overbook on each flight, how many to release at each discount fare, and how to manage connecting traffic across the network. The results combine into the inventory levels the reservation system enforces.

What changed, by American's estimate:
- $1.4 billion in quantifiable benefit over three years
- more than $500 million a year expected to continue
- the practice the whole industry now calls revenue management

It won the 1991 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of model for a distributor deciding which orders to accept and which to quote at what price, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your sales team still decides what to promise and at what price from instinct, we'd like to hear how.

evidence.title:
Samsung Electronics cut the time to make a memory chip from more than 80 days to less than 30. The authors estimate it brought in an additional $1 billion in sales revenue, because memory chip prices fall so fast that a chip sold a month earlier sells for more.

A memory chip goes through more than 400 fabrication steps. In December 1995, a Berkeley benchmarking team found that one of Samsung's lines had excellent yields and productivity, but the longest cycle time of 29 fabs it had surveyed. Each line worked to a monthly output target, with supervisors pushing through whatever work was needed to make that month's number, and work in process had built up across the floor.

From 1996 to 1999, Samsung's managers worked with Robert Leachman of UC Berkeley and his consulting firm on SLIM. It sets a target cycle time and work-in-process level for every manufacturing step, schedules the floor to keep the bottleneck photolithography machines supplied with work, and uses optimization to check capacity. It started on two of the six lines at Kiheung and reached all of Samsung's fab lines by March 1998.

What changed, by the authors' count:
- time to fabricate memory chips down from more than 80 days to less than 30
- an additional $1 billion in sales revenue from March 1996 to December 2000, against a no-SLIM baseline
- on-time delivery at electrical die sort up from 70 to 96 percent
- Samsung's share of the memory chip market up from 18 to 22 percent during the project

It was a finalist for the 2001 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of scheduling model for a plant with three lines and a few dozen steps, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team runs the floor to a monthly output target, we'd like to hear how you decide what runs next.

evidence.title:
From mid-1999 through autumn 2000, Canadian Pacific Railway saved C$300 million (US$170 million), by its own count, after it began running its freight trains to a schedule built with optimization models.

Like most North American railways at the time, CP dispatched by tonnage: a train left when enough freight had built up to fill it. That keeps the number of trains low, but crews, locomotives and railcars end up waiting on each other, and customers get uncertain delivery times. Moving a 14,000-mile network onto a fixed schedule means deciding how cars are grouped into blocks, which trains carry each block, and where locomotives and empty cars need to be.

CP's planners worked with MultiModal Applied Systems on a set of decision-support tools. They combine an optimal block-sequencing algorithm, a heuristic for designing blocks, very fast simulation, and time-space network models that plan locomotive use and the distribution of empty cars. The operating plan was matched to traffic patterns, with contingency plans for high- and low-volume days.

What changed, by CP's count:
- C$300 million saved from mid-1999 through autumn 2000, and at least C$210 million more estimated in fuel and labor alone in 2001 and 2002
- Labor productivity up 40% and locomotive productivity up 35%
- Fuel consumption improved by 17%
- Railcar velocity up 41%

It won the 2003 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of scheduled operating plan for a regional carrier running fixed lanes between four terminals, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team sends a truck or a train once there's enough freight to fill it, we'd like to hear how you decide when to go.

evidence.originalText:
From mid-1999 through autumn 2000, Canadian Pacific Railway saved C$300 million (US$170 million), by its own count, after it began running its freight trains to a schedule built with optimization models.

Like most North American railways at the time, CP dispatched by tonnage: a train left when enough freight had built up to fill it. That keeps the number of trains low, but crews, locomotives and railcars end up waiting on each other, and customers get uncertain delivery times. Moving a 14,000-mile network onto a fixed schedule means deciding how cars are grouped into blocks, which trains carry each block, and where locomotives and empty cars need to be.

CP's planners worked with MultiModal Applied Systems on a set of decision-support tools. They combine an optimal block-sequencing algorithm, a heuristic for designing blocks, very fast simulation, and time-space network models that plan locomotive use and the distribution of empty cars. The operating plan was matched to traffic patterns, with contingency plans for high- and low-volume days.

What changed, by CP's count:
- C$300 million saved from mid-1999 through autumn 2000, and at least C$210 million more estimated in fuel and labor alone in 2001 and 2002
- Labor productivity up 40% and locomotive productivity up 35%
- Fuel consumption improved by 17%
- Railcar velocity up 41%

It won the 2003 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of scheduled operating plan for a regional carrier running fixed lanes between four terminals, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team sends a truck or a train once there's enough freight to fill it, we'd like to hear how you decide when to go.

evidence.title:
From 2007 through 2010, the Midwest grid run by MISO saved between $2.1 billion and $3.0 billion, by MISO's estimate. The savings came from markets that use optimization to decide which power plants run and how much each one produces.

US utilities historically focused on their own service areas, making the most of their own plants and transmission lines, and trading power with neighbors was hard. MISO, approved as the first regional transmission organization in 2001, coordinates more than 1,500 power plants and over 55,000 miles of transmission lines. Choosing the cheapest set of plants that meets demand without overloading any line is a very large scheduling problem.

MISO's team built its markets with Alstom Grid, Utilicast and AIMMS, among others. A mixed-integer program decides when each power plant should be on or off; further optimization models set output levels and the prices at which energy trades. The energy market opened in April 2005, and the combined energy and ancillary services markets in January 2009. Every five minutes, MISO tells plants how much to produce, selecting the lowest-cost producers that meet demand within the system's limits.

What changed, by MISO's count:
- $2.1 billion to $3.0 billion in cumulative savings across the region, 2007 to 2010
- A further $6.1 billion to $8.1 billion expected through 2020
- Better use of existing plants and lines, a more reliable grid and less need for new infrastructure
- $24 billion in transactions cleared in 2009

It won the 2011 Franz Edelman Award, the top prize in operations research.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of on/off scheduling model for a site running its own generators, boilers or chillers against the power price, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your team sets tomorrow's unit schedule from experience and a price forecast, we'd like to hear how you decide what runs.

evidence.title:
Since January 2020, a model that combines subsidized taxi rides into shared routes has cut 15 million driving kilometers a year in the Netherlands, and saved 60 million euros from 2019 to 2023, by the project team's conservative estimates.

About 200,000 elderly and disabled people a year use subsidized long-distance taxi rides run by Transvision. On a single day there can be up to 15,000 rides to plan. That planning used to be split across dozens of subcontractors, each working on its own share. Planning it together means deciding which passengers can share a taxi, in what order they are picked up and dropped off, and how the routes are spread over more than 60 taxi operators, while keeping to promised times for a vulnerable group of passengers.

Transvision built the system with the Eindhoven consultancy CQM and the geo-information company Geodan. It plans each day's rides in one batch, anywhere from 1,000 to 15,000 of them, using dial-a-ride heuristics run in parallel, plus new ways to compute the millions to billions of distances and driving times it needs on the Dutch road network. It also had to cope with changing regulations and COVID-19 measures along the way.

What changed, by the project team's count:
- 15 million fewer driving kilometers a year
- 60 million euros saved for all stakeholders combined over 2019 to 2023, with another 30 million euros projected for 2024 and 2025
- Better punctuality and a 50% improvement in passenger satisfaction

It was a finalist for the 2024 Franz Edelman Award.

That's the gap we work on at OpEra: the same kind of ride-pooling model for a patient-transport or shuttle operator with 40 vehicles, built in weeks on the data it already has.

If your dispatchers combine the next day's bookings into routes by hand, we'd like to hear how you decide who rides together.

most builders using it now are already technical. but the real play? non-technical people who learn just enough to orchestrate agents w
evidence.text:
claude code wrappers are the next big thing

most builders using it now are already technical. but the real play? non-technical people who learn just enough to orchestrate agents without writing everything from scratch

the wrapper layer is where money gets made. salesforce is a wrapper. cursor is a wrapper. lovable is a wrapper.

people who build interfaces on top of powerful-but-awkward tools print money

if you spend 6 months getting comfortable with claude code, building small agents, understanding how to chain them - you'll be positioned when businesses start wanting "AI agents" without knowing what that means

they'll pay 2-5k/month for something you can build in hours once you know the patterns

the gap between what AI can do and what business owners understand is the entire opportunity

evidence.title:
(3/5) it's not just a one-off glitch. two different biases show up

the first one is position. if you swap which option comes first, the winner flips even when the content is ident
evidence.text:
(3/5) it's not just a one-off glitch. two different biases show up

the first one is position. if you swap which option comes first, the winner flips even when the content is identical. i tried people's names instead of A and B so there was no alphabet to lean on, and whoever got listed first still won. line up six copies of the same thing and the first slot alone takes about 91% of the probability

the second is the label text itself. call them fork A and fork B and A usually wins, even from second place. it isn't that A is magic either: earlier-looking labels keep winning across other pairs too

so jev can look extremely confident for reasons that have nothing to do with the actual content. kind of crazy the training data didn't train these biases out. i really hope nobody is using this to rank job applicants

evidence.title: (5/5) none of this makes jev useless. it's still the fastest, cheapest judge i've run (235ms, $0.0059 for 360 calls, matched sonnet on sabotaged diffs at ~1/50th the cost). it just
evidence.text:
(5/5) none of this makes jev useless. it's still the fastest, cheapest judge i've run (235ms, $0.0059 for 360 calls, matched sonnet on sabotaged diffs at ~1/50th the cost). it just has one rule: the option set has to contain the truth

how i'm running it now:

1. put the true answer in the options ("same", "neither", "not enough info"). 24/24 on the sabotage set in one call
2. ask twice, swap positions, average. kills leftover prior on close calls (~$0.0002 a race)
3. tests decide, jev ranks. high scores (0.90+) are right ~98% of the time. mid scores (0.50–0.70) fall to ~17%. take the probabilities with a pinch of salt

evidence.text:
Putting together a proper bench so stay tuned for that! But we do beat them on durable writes.

Until we raise 1B dollars, going to be tough to compete on the cold start 😄. Also, we have dynamic memory limits, which makes doing what CF isolates do very tough.

Still, our cold start P95 is 334ms. Which isn't a big deal for background tasks + if it's a user initiated task, a quick ack such as a slack reaction can almost fully cover the latency.

There is some tech coming out soon that may help us get this down as well though. So it will keep getting better!

It surveyed more than 5,000 Americans who saw a primary care doctor this year,
evidence.text:
Doctors think patients are scared of AI in healthcare, but Gallup just showed they’ve got it wrong.

It surveyed more than 5,000 Americans who saw a primary care doctor this year, and asked if they’d be comfortable with AI making diagnosis and treatment decisions as long as their doctor could change or override them.

56% said yes, but when Gallup asked over 1,000 primary care providers how many patients would feel that way, they guessed only 36%.

And there’s a catch, because when there’s no doctor reviewing the AI at all, patient comfort drops to just 9%.

So patients aren’t against AI, they just want a doctor checking it. And that’s how AI in healthcare should be built, with the AI doing the work and the doctor keeping the final say.

It’s called AWS Emulator, a free copy of Amazon’s cloud tools that developers can run on their laptop, and thou
evidence.text:
Amazon just released software that no human wrote or even reviewed.

It’s called AWS Emulator, a free copy of Amazon’s cloud tools that developers can run on their laptop, and thousands of AI agents wrote every line of it.

Here’s how they pulled it off →
→ One team of agents writes tests, each checked against the real Amazon cloud first
 → A second team runs those tests and files every failure
 → A third team fixes one issue at a time
 → Nothing gets merged until it passes checks for the build, security and accuracy
 → Humans set the rules, and stepped in when one agent built its own Python interpreter from scratch

So what made this work was a test that tells the agents clearly when they’re right and when they’re wrong.

And that’s the whole idea behind RL, because an agent only gets better when something scores its work honestly, and the better that score, the more you can trust the agent.

evidence.title:
Pharma giants guard their lab data like nuclear codes.

That’s because it holds decades of experiments, billions of dollars of research and every drug they’ve ever tested. So it’s
evidence.text:
Pharma giants guard their lab data like nuclear codes.

That’s because it holds decades of experiments, billions of dollars of research and every drug they’ve ever tested. So it’s the one thing they never share.

But 10 of them, including AstraZeneca, GSK, Novartis, Bayer and Amgen, fed it into the same AI anyway. That came to more than 2.6 billion lab results.

And none of them saw each other’s data. Each company trained its own copy of the AI inside its own walls, and only what each copy learned was combined into one model.

The result was that all 10 got better models than they had alone, especially at spotting which drugs could be toxic. That matters because a toxic drug caught early saves years of work and millions of dollars.

It worked because every failed experiment is a lesson. A compound that turned out harmful tells the AI what not to try next.

Now imagine being an AI startup in drug discovery. You can rent computing power, use the best models and hire great people, but you can’t buy 2.6 billion experiments.

So who wins the next 10 years in AI, the companies with the best models or the ones with the most data?

A lo
evidence.text:
AI is about to run out of internet.

Researchers estimate that, if current trends continue, the good public text online will be fully used up somewhere between 2026 and 2032.

A lot of people read that as AI slowing down.

But it means the opposite, because a lot of the most useful knowledge in the world was never online in the first place.

→ How a nurse calms a panicking patient on the phone
 → How a mechanic hears what’s wrong with an engine before opening it
 → How a lab knows which experiments never to try again
 → How a good salesperson knows when to stop talking
 → How a chef knows the dish is ready without a timer

Almost none of this is written down in a way AI can learn from. So far, AI has learned mostly from what people wrote.

Next, it has to learn from what people do, and someone has to go out and record that.

So the next great AI companies won’t be the ones with the biggest models. They’ll be the ones who collect what the internet never had.

evidence.text:
Being a traditional scientist doesn't work. Being a traditional founder doesn't work. Following anything traditional will get you nowhere. Being authentically you is what works. You have to think outside the bubble, whatever bubble you're in. The world doesn't revolve around the bubble you see; it's so diverse. 
So how do you get out of it? By allowing yourself to open your mind and talk to people, and by learning that rules don't define how you should think. That's how you find your voice and burst the bubble: by forcing yourself to do uncomfortable things, so many time I had to do this.
So little credit is given to being uncomfortable, because it's so risky, right?

evidence.title: Saccade (F26) | World's Earliest Test for Alzheimer's Biomarkers
evidence.text:
We are the World's Earliest Test for Alzheimer's Biomarkers.

Alzheimer's testing today is bottlenecked around the onset of symptoms, when the damage is already done. 

Current treatments, including the FDA-approved drugs released in 2024, don't reverse the disease; they only slow it down. Earlier detection means earlier intervention.

Eye movement changes linked to Alzheimer's surface sooner than any other biomarker, up to 15 years before symptoms appear.

We deliver a 15-minute VR assessment delivered to patients in longevity clinics:
 

• Tasks: patients perform visual tasks designed by neurologists to trigger a distinct oculomotor response in people with Alzheimer's or on its path
 
• Hardware: our patent-pending attachment connects to any VR headset on the market and captures these eye movement patterns.

• Analysis: the patterns are compared against our ML model to produce a risk analysis.

Once classified, patients can access new interventions, such as the FDA-approved drugs.

They're also referred to longevity practices, neurology practices or both, depending on their stage of decline.

Testing for the earliest biomarkers allows the earliest possible intervention.

In some cases, that slows the disease enough that patients outlive the onset of symptoms and never face memory loss in their lifetime.

evidence.title: Workers IO - Deterministic Simulation Testing
evidence.text:
Workers IO is building deterministic simulation environments to verify mission-critical systems.

AI agents can now write years’ worth of code in days, but it still takes significant engineering hours to verify what’s being built.

The slowest part of engineering now is verification.

Teams need to understand how different parts of their system work together and what happens as they fail and recover. It’s often impossible to predict all scenarios that could lead to a failure and that’s why most expensive failures are found in production.

Workers IO runs millions of simulated production scenarios on your entire system, including dependencies. These simulations take place inside a deterministic hypervisor which injects faults like network delays, disk errors, and process failures to verify how your system handles these conditions.

Deterministic execution allows you to perfectly reproduce scenarios, giving your agents rich context to inspect failures and work on fixing them. This allows teams to do years’ worth of testing in days and build confidence in what they’re shipping.

evidence.title: Canos (YC F26) | A Blood Test to Detect Pet Cancer Earlier
evidence.text:
Canos (YC F26) is building a blood test to detect pet cancer earlier.

1 in 4 dogs will develop cancer in their lifetime, and most cases are caught late, because dogs can’t tell us when something feels wrong. Routine bloodwork rarely gives an answer, and advanced imaging like CT is costly and requiring sedation. Vets need tools that not only detect cancer, but also show where it is and what type it is, so they know exactly what to do next.

We are bringing the standard of human liquid biopsy to veterinary medicine. Canos detects and tracks cancer from a single blood draw using cell-free DNA sequencing. Instead of measuring a single biomarker or a panel of mutations, we read the whole-genome signal and analyze 500+ multimodal features, including methylation patterns, one of the most robust signals for cancer detection and enables prediction of cancer location, metastasis and remission. In a benchmark study of 896 samples from 341 dogs, our model reached 91% sensitivity and 95% specificity, and it gets better with every new sample.

Over time, this builds something rare: records of the same dogs from health, to cancer, to treatment. Dogs age roughly 7 times faster than humans and their cancers often progress within a year, so what takes decades to observe in people unfolds in a few years. Because dogs develop cancer naturally and share our homes, this data can unlock breakthroughs in cancer and aging research for dogs and humans alike.

Mingshan Tsai (PhD, Zoology) and Bin Li (PhD, Machine Learning) are Oxford scientists and lifelong animal lovers. At their previous company, ZYTCA, they built an AI pathology platform for pet cancer in 6 months. They took Canos from idea to working prototype in 3 months, validating the workflow on their own blood, and have already shared their first scientific paper.

#Canos #DogCancer #LiquidBiopsy #PetHealth #YCombinator

Why did Y Combinator back us to build technology for your parents?

Because we believe the next generation of technology shouldn't just be built for the young.

For nearly 20 years, our family cared for loved ones at home. We saw firsthand how much of aging isn't about needing someone to do everything for you. It's about needing a little help with the everyday things.

evidence.title: Perit - expert led datasets for frontier labs
evidence.text:
Meet Perit (YC F26), expert-led datasets for frontier AI labs.

Every major AI lab is racing to build models that can hear, see, reason and act in the real world. The bottleneck isn't compute anymore. It's high-quality, expert-made data. Perit builds that data across four verticals:

🎙️ Voice: natural, multilingual conversational audio for training voice models
🎥 Egocentric video: first-person footage of real-world tasks for robotics and embodied AI
🧠 RL environments: expert-designed environments and tasks for reinforcement learning
🏢 Enterprise data: real-world, domain-specific data from professionals

Our AI-powered onboarding and QA let us source, vet and manage thousands of expert contributors worldwide, so labs get data that's accurate, diverse and ready to train on.

🛒 Introducing the Perit Marketplace: Got data? Whether it's audio, video, documents, code or something else entirely, you can submit it at https://perit.ai/marketplace and we'll help put it in front of the AI labs that need it. Turn the data you already have into revenue.

We already work with most of the frontier labs, and we've closed $11M in revenue in our first 4.5 months.

Perit was founded by siblings Kshitij Dixit (CEO) and Poorva Dixit (CTO), who are both IIT Kharagpur alumni and 2x YC founders. They previously built Zeo to millions of drivers across 100+ countries and millions of dollars in revenue. Poorva comes from big tech, with stints at Google Cloud AI, Uber, Atlassian and Flipkart.

🔗 Learn more: https://perit.ai/
🛒 Submit your data: https://perit.ai/marketplace
📩 Labs and partners, reach out at support@perit.ai

#AI #MachineLearning #TrainingData #YCombinator #Robotics #VoiceAI #DataMarketplace

evidence.title: Meet Lark: AI agents for distributors
evidence.text:
At Lark, we deploy AI agents for distributors that help with sales, inventory and purchasing.

Quotes: customer requests come in, and Lark drafts the quote for your team to approve.
Inventory: it tracks demand, spots trends, and factors in seasonality and minimum order quantities. It doesn't take vacations.
Chat: ask it anything in plain English, and it runs the analysis and gives you insights.

Faster quotes, less typing, fewer stockouts, and less cash tied up in stock.

Jason Wang and Michael Wang, co-founders
